# Just Once

> "Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes that plunder the vineyards; for our vineyards are in blossom."
>
> — Song of Solomon 2:15

## Do not negotiate {-}

A woman has a pursuer who will not stop calling. She ignores his messages, thirty of them. Then, worn out, she calls him back, only to tell him to leave her alone. It makes no difference what she says. He has learned what it costs to reach her. It costs thirty messages.

That picture comes from Gavin de Becker, an American security specialist who spent his career guarding public figures from stalkers. He put it in a book called *The Gift of Fear*, in 1997. He has one rule for every kind of unwanted pursuit, and it is three words long. Do not negotiate.

His instructions to the woman are worth knowing for their own sake. There are four.

Say it once, and say it outright. She tells him that she has no interest in him and is certain she never will, whatever he may have assumed until now.

Give no reason. A reason is something he can argue with. If she says she doesn't want a relationship "right now", the only words he hears are "right now". A refusal with a condition attached is a discussion.

Don't let him down gently. A kindness that leaves the door open an inch is heard as hope.

Then never answer again. She doesn't answer the angry call, or the apology, or the "one last goodbye". She doesn't send a friend to warn him off. Every reply of any kind buys her weeks more of the same. "The way to stop contact", de Becker wrote, "is to stop contact." And if she is ever afraid of him, she goes to the police.

De Becker himself reaches for the comparison this book needs. The pursuer, he says, is like an addict, and she is the drug. Small doses don't wean him. They keep him hooked. The only cure is none at all.

Now hear that list from the other side, because some man reading this is the caller. You wouldn't call yourself a stalker. You would say that you're persistent, or in love, or that she never gave you a fair chance. Here is how it looks from where she stands. She said no, and she meant it. Every message since then has frightened her a little more. Each one tells her that her no counts for nothing with you. That isn't love. Love wants her good, and she has told you what her good is. What keeps you dialing is the thing this whole book is about. It is wanting, and it has you by the collar.

So the cure is the same for you. Stop contact. Send no last message, no apology and no explanation. Don't drive past her house, and don't look at her pictures. It will feel unbearable for a few days, and it is only the itch. In many places what you are doing is also a crime. If you find you can't stop, tell a doctor or a counselor today.

For every other reader, turn the picture around. De Becker was writing about dangerous men, and he could have been writing about your habit.

You have a caller of your own. This book calls him the Little Monster, and you should keep his size in view. He is an itch. That is all he is. He is about as strong as a mosquito bite, or a tag scratching at the back of your collar. He can't hurt you, and he can't make you do anything. He can only nag. Left alone, he nags a little less each day, and then he is gone.

Nobody ever went back because the itch was unbearable. It isn't. If stopping has ever felt like torture to you, the itch wasn't doing it. The wanting was, and the belief that you were being denied something. Men go back because they believe "just once" will buy them some peace.

It buys the opposite. Hold out for ten days and then give in "just once", and you have not bought any peace. You have taught the Little Monster that ten days of nagging gets him fed. Next time he will nag for eleven, quite cheerfully.

So take de Becker's advice. Say No once, and leave no hope in it. This book will bring you to that moment, and it is one plain No. After that, don't pick up. Don't argue with the itch, and don't bargain with it. Arguing is answering. An itch that is never answered has nothing to learn, and it stops calling.

## Three doors {-}

"Just once" is a myth. Get it out of your head. It gets into a man's life by three doors, and they are worth knowing.

The first door is how every one of us began. No boy ever decided on a habit of twenty years. He decided on once.

The second door is the attempt to stop. A man is four days in and doing well. Then comes a rough week, or a special occasion, and he allows himself one to get through it. That attempt is over. Look back at your own. Most of them were not beaten by a hundred nights. They were beaten by one.

The third door is the cruelest. It opens for a man who has been free for months, or for years. He does it once to prove he doesn't need it anymore, or simply to see. It proves the opposite.

Men say afterward that the habit "came back". It didn't come back by itself. It was let in, once.

## What one buys {-}

Ask what the one actually delivers.

If the Little Monster is still alive, it buys a few minutes of quiet, and it teaches him how long he has to nag. If he is long dead, it buys nothing at all. A free man has no itch to relieve. He gets ten flat minutes and feels like a fool.

What follows is always the same. The flatness lands, and it's so grim that the man is certain nothing this miserable could ever hook him again.

But it already has.

Within a day or two the pull for another one arrives. Men call it the chaser. The caller got through, and now he is ringing again. The man sits there baffled that a thing which makes him feel this bad could have made him do it. Yet it did.

John Owen, an English pastor, wrote in 1656 that sin "aims always at the utmost". It never wants one. It asks for one in order to get the rest.

## The special one {-}

You know the voice that sells it. It says it's just one more time, just one more video, and you can get back to your purpose after. It always sounds that reasonable, and it always promises that you can go straight back to being the man you meant to be.

It's the thought of one special time that stops many men from ever stopping. The one after a week away on business. The one after the fight. The one on the night she turns over and says she's tired. The one video. The one message to her, "just to say hello". The one you've "earned".

Notice what the voice never offers. It never says, "Go back to doing this every night for another twenty years." No man would take that offer. So it offers one, because one is the only size it can sell.

Get this fixed in your mind: JUST ONCE DOES NOT EXIST. It's a chain, and each link is forged by the one before. The myth of the rare special occasion is also what keeps men moping after they've quit. They are like a man who has moved to a new house and keeps driving past the old one.

## See the whole of it {-}

So train yourself never to picture the single, harmless time. It's a fantasy in every sense. When lust comes to mind, see the whole of it. See thousands of locked doors and thousands of flat ten minutes afterward. See a secret carried through every room you walk into, and the years of your strength poured down a drain. A weak moment isn't a crime. But why choose a lifetime of that, when you could be free?

And when the voice comes, remember the rule. Do not negotiate. You don't have to win the argument, because there isn't one. A man who is debating whether tonight is an exception has already picked up the phone.

Don't frighten yourself with any of this. You can do it. Any man can. It's absurdly easy, so long as you have three things straight:

1. There is nothing to give up. There is only a great deal to gain.
2. There is no harmless one. There is only the whole chain or none of it.
3. When you give your answer, you give it once. After that, you don't reopen the question.

## The little fox {-}

The Song of Solomon is a love poem in the Bible, and it has a line for this: "Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes that plunder the vineyards". It doesn't warn about wolves. It warns about little foxes. Nobody loses a vineyard to a wolf. The damage is done by something small enough to slip under the fence while the vines are in flower.

"Just once" is the little fox.
